A Living Legacy: Carte Blanche Making a Difference Trust

By: Laura Byrne | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
As the Trust heads into its 18th year, we celebrate its work and recognise the contributions of donors and partners in its coming of age.

Unique Selling Point:
The Trust turns 18 next year, in 2026. Its latest project (a neonatal unit at George Provincial Hospital) will be completed to coincide with the birthday. We reflect on the lives touched, communities served and stories told. We celebrate the leap of faith that donors and partners make with us, and the idea that all of us are a brick in the wall, contributing towards projects that are always more than the sum of their parts.


Summary:
The Carte Blanche Making a Difference Trust was founded in 2008 for the show’s twentieth birthday. It builds and equips dedicated paediatric facilities in state hospitals, filling gaps in care such as burns treatment, emergency and trauma units, operating theatres, and so on.

Behind everything the Trust does is its Patron, Karolina Andropoulos. Her daughter Georgina died aged seven of cancer in 2008, after many years of treatment both in South Africa and in Australia. After her death, Karolina became driven to help create support for South African children in state hospitals similar to what had been available in Australia. Karolina approached George and asked him to tour Charlotte Maxeke’s paediatric unit with her to see what was needed, and so the Trust was born.

The initial idea was to raise funds to contribute towards equipment for a local hospital. What it turned into was multiple projects in hospitals all over South Africa - not only equipment donations, but building and equipping operating theatres, centres of excellence and so on.

Carte Blanche periodically features the Trust’s work in stories - usually at the handover of a new project - partly because the Trust’s ongoing success and ability to raise funds is dependent on its association with the Carte Blanche brand, and partly to recognise the incredible contributions of donors and partners. Several companies have donated many millions of rands over the past two decades, many of them more than once, and numerous professionals and their companies have donated time, skills and materials.

Further information:
More immediately, the Trust has recently completed three projects at Ngwelezana Hospital in KZN (incidentally, the province is the Trust’s largest beneficiary over time). These are focused on treatment of burns: an inpatient unit, an outpatient unit, and state-of-the-art equipment for testing, cleaning wounds and performing skin grafts. However, there has been increasing difficulty in dealing with the Department of Health in KZN, which has blocked Carte Blanche from hosting a handover of the new facilities to the hospital (and the province). As a result, we have not been able to celebrate our contributors and the finalisation of the project as we usually do.

This is primarily why MultiChoice (which is a significant supporter of the Trust’s work, and whose CEO is a Trustee) commissioned a special piece from Carte Blanche to recognise the contribution of the donors and partners in the Ngwelezana projects, to be extended to a celebration of all the people and companies who have contributed over the years.

We will interview about 10 “A List” contributors as provided by Karolina. Further details below.
In addition we will incorporate “vox pops” from some side characters such as Carte Blanche producers and presenters who have worked on Trust stories, doctors and nurses at the hospitals etc.

We will return to two hospitals, hopefully:
1. Charlotte Maxeke, as the site of the genesis of the Trust.
The Trust completed a few projects there in its early years (2008-2011): installation of a heart-lung machine, installation of a Lodox digital scanner, and installation of a laparoscopic operating theatre. The operating theatre is still well used and well kept, and we will hopefully return to talk about the impact of this facility on the department. Although staff who were there in 2008-11 have since left, a new generation can use the same facilities to create a better chance for the children in their care.
2. Victoria Mxenge (previously King Edward VIII), Durban, as a representative of KZN and a major focus for the Trust over more than one project. The Trust has contributed equipment to the neonatal nursery, and most importantly, constructed a brand new Paediatric Centre of Excellence (2012). Prof Kimesh Naidoo has worked at the hospital since the Trust’s earliest projects there, and his career has spanned many of the new facilities and capabilities provided by the Trust. He will provide a great legacy interview.


Extra Budget Items:
Travel and accommodation for 1-2 days' shoot in Durban and Richards Bay

Script:


Part 1

(Peter Grealy) These are undeniably world-class facilities.



(Benjamin Mokgothu Subtitles) Ours is to create a healing environment and a working space for health professionals to take care of those little ones who need healthcare.



(Claire Mawisa) First of its kind facilities, world class care. Would you believe that all of this could be possible behind the unpromising facade of a decades-old government hospital?



(Claire Mawisa) But it’s in just such places that a dream has been unfolding for nearly two decades.



(Braam van der Hoven) We don't need to fix everything in one go; we can just start. And it will grow.



(Claire Mawisa) A dream to provide dedicated, specialist healthcare to children who depend on state hospitals.



(Claire Mawisa) Seventeen years on, the Carte Blanche Making a Difference Trust has raised over R200 million, completed 24 projects across 6 provinces, and made a difference to more than 500 000 children. And it all started here, at Charlotte Maxeke Johannesburg Academic Hospital.



(Karolina Andropoulos) This is the big deal. For me, this is the big deal.



(Dr Tanusha Ramdin) There was nothing here. There was no cubicles. It was completely empty.

.

(Claire Mawisa) Dr Tanusha Ramdin is head of the neonatal unit. She was a registrar when the Trust built the hospital’s first specialised pediatric unit.



(Dr Tanusha Ramdin) I’ve seen the project grow and what a huge impact it’s made on our children. You can see, years later, we’re still working at it. This is our way of preventing the spread of infections. So, it’s made a huge difference.



(Claire Mawisa) In 2008, Carte Blanche was celebrating a major milestone.



(Derek Watts) Carte Blanche turns 20 this month and there’s a lot to celebrate. But it’s not all about partying.



(Claire Mawisa) Then-Executive Producer, George Mazarakis, aimed to mark the anniversary in an unusual way.



(George Mazarakis) I think it’s time to press pause on the critical button and to say now’s the time to actually make a difference and say, how can we help?



(Claire Mawisa) For Karolina Andropoulos, it was a significant year for a very different reason.



(Karolina Andropoulos) I lost a little girl called Georgina. I was terribly moved by, of course, my daughter first, but all the other children I’d seen in state facilities.



(Derek Watts) And that’s probably why you identify so strongly with these mothers and their babies, their toddlers.



(Karolina Andropoulos) Love them all dearly, they… When you become one of these parents, I think it’s beyond empathy.



(Claire Mawisa) Karolina’s daughter Georgina is the muse behind the Trust. She died in April 2008. She was an outpatient at Charlotte Maxeke.



(Karolina Andropoulos) I approached George Mazarakis and asked him to join me in this hospital, which he did. And he thereafter, together with a cohort of specialists, founded the Carte Blanche Making a Difference Trust.



(George Mazarakis) My dream is to reach R20 million - a million for every year we’ve been on air. I think that would be a meaningful contribution.



(Claire Mawisa) And so the first projects took shape.



(Narrator) Suspended from the ceiling is the latest in high-definition technology.



(Narrator) In Bara’s surgical neonatal unit, the Trust has made a massive impact, revamping the entire area. But it’s not finished yet.



(Derek Watts) So Karolina, five ICU beds, what are we looking at?



(Karolina Andropoulos) At about R2.5 million please.



(Prof. Millind Chitnis) It is really impressive. It is not only of national standard, it is of international standard.



(Bongani Bingwa) So this is it?



(Gordon Monchu) This is our pediatric ICU for Kimberley Hospital. When I walked in the first time, I couldn’t help myself, I just saw tears rolling down because of the good work and the goodwill that went into this.



(Narrator) The Carte Blanche Making a Difference Trust then used half a million rand from viewers to create a comprehensive preschool.



(Claire Mawisa) From the very beginning, the Trust has achieved more than anyone could have dreamed.



(Claire Mawisa) Did you ever imagine that 200 million would be raised?



(Chris Nel) Honestly, nobody expected that to happen.



(Claire Mawisa) Chris Nel is the Trust’s financial architect.



(Chris Nel) Our expectations were too little. The funds just started rolling in, and we had to ensure that our trust, our methods and our systems, adjusted and was flexible enough to accommodate the growth.



(Claire Mawisa) So those were good problems to have.



(Chris Nel) Yes, they were good problems to have.



(Claire Mawisa) Absolutely.



(Claire Mawisa) And what began as a birthday celebration has become nearly eighteen years of touching lives.



(Chris Nel) The donors not only gave us money, but they actually gave us trust.



(Claire Mawisa) Beyond the balance sheets, what is it like being part of the journey from day one?



(Chris Nel) It has been very honoring for me. My whole life I was involved with figures and sums. But this, although it also had to do with the rands and cents, it had a total different meaning. Every decision that we take has a heartbeat behind it.



(Peter Grealy) What is unique about the Carte Blanche Making a Difference Trust is that every cent of the capital donations that have been made to us have been applied to our projects.



(Claire Mawisa) Peter Grealy has been a Trustee and the Trust’s legal advisor since the very beginning.



(Peter Grealy) We've carved out a methodology that ensures that there's no wastage. And that's an important message I think in the South African context, that if you're absolutely focused on the outcome, that it is achievable.



(Gladys Bogoshi) Without the partnership of the private sector, the NGOs, we cannot meet our mandate.



(Claire Mawisa) Gladys Bogoshi is the CEO of Charlotte Maxeke Academic Hospital.



(Gladys Bogoshi) To have this vision in 2011, to build this unit from the shell…



(George Mazarakis) This is the very first pediatric specialised ICU in Gauteng, outside of neonatal.



(Gladys Bogoshi) …and to come back today. I hope you are proud that it has saved so many lives and it still does.



(Dr Tanusha Ramdin) We actually serve, like, half of Gauteng. The patient next door is a trauma patient. The patient next door there is a burns patient. So, we try and accommodate everybody.



(Karolina Andropoulos) Fourteen years later, it's still immaculate and in service. And it's enchanting to know that you, as a young baby doctor, a registrar working here 14 years ago, are now the head of neonatology. It's a beautiful thing.



(Claire Mawisa) This has always been more than philanthropy. It's the belief that the health of our nation's children is a shared responsibility, and by building these havens of hope, we’re building a healthier future for everyone.

Part 2
(Claire Mawisa) In any hospital, there are stories of pain, struggle, and fear. What the Making a Difference Trust sets out to do is to change the endings of those stories.



(Nomsa Piliso) So, I mean, stories - the way that we think about storytelling, one is to preserve our history and also to weave ourselves into the national psyche.



(Claire Mawisa) MultiChoice’s Nomsa Piliso is a trustee.



(Nomsa Piliso) The community in and of itself and corporate should not stand back. If you understand that everybody has a contribution to make, then the model works.



(Claire Mawisa) And that’s exactly what unfolded at Victoria Mxenge Hospital in Durban.



(Prof. Kimesh Naidoo) Public sector patients are often seen as, oh, they can get something lesser. And this was not done here. We said we’re going to give the kids the best infrastructure there is to offer, and that makes a huge difference.



(Dr Kimesh Naidoo) What happened? You woke up now? You woke up?



(Claire Mawisa) In 2008, Professor Kimesh Naidoo was simply Doctor Naidoo, a pediatrician at what was then called King Edward VIII.



(Dr Kimesh Naidoo) I think looking after sick children in a derelict building which has not been planned appropriately is very dangerous.



(Claire Mawisa) It was here, at the hospital where Professor Naidoo still works, that the Trust pulled off one of its most ambitious projects.



(George Mazarakis) King Edward stood out head and shoulders above the rest in terms of a place where we needed to intervene to the degree of building a new building, purely because it was so shocking.



(Claire Mawisa) The BHP Billiton Pediatric Centre of Excellence was completed in 2012.



(Narrator) Gone was the old, cramped outpatients’ area. In its place, a spacious waiting room with a dispensary, clean toilets and consulting rooms attached.



(Bongani Bingwa) And that’s the whole point of this hospital, is that these spaces are made to work - not only for the doctors and the nursing staff, but for the patients as well. And these little guys are what it’s all about. Go!



(Claire Mawisa) What do you think have been probably the biggest changes that this center has been able to impact on?



(Prof. Kimesh Naidoo) The ability to look after children, especially ICU children, children in high care, in a clean, safe environment where they're not packed together, where there's enough equipment. We have treated over 340,000 children who have come in mainly as outpatients and about 10 to 15% of them, just under 35,000, have been admitted. And these are some of the sickest children in the entire province who have had to be admitted here.



(Claire Mawisa) Thirteen years later, the centre continues to transform lives - and has provided training to a new generation of pediatric specialists.



(Prof. Kimesh Naidoo) There's a pride in the place. It's beautiful. It's a centre of focus in the hospital. We were all sitting in 2012 and you could hear the stories: How long will it last? Will the government manage to keep it going? And I think it's really a team effort that enables something that's donated, something that's given, to be looked after and to fulfill its duty and fulfill its mandate. We’re proud that we've done that. And we will continue to do that.



(Claire Mawisa) A child born when these projects began is on the cusp of adulthood. And so is the Trust. But its legacy isn't measured in years - or in money. It’s measured in breaths. In the steady beep of a monitor that’s in a unit that didn’t exist before.



(Claire Mawisa) And that legacy is shared by partners both past and present.



(Braam van der Hoven) It's wonderful to go back and to see that the upkeep on these facilities is good because there's ownership.



(Claire Mawisa) Braam van der Hoven was the lead architect on the Victoria Mxenge project - and many others.



(Braam van der Hoven) My function is to balance the requirements of the clinicians with the available budget and space, and then to come up with a design solution that will shorten the length of stay of the patients in these facilities. We sort of do that through natural light and colourful interiors that brings a calming effect to the patients and the caregivers.



(Braam van der Hoven) On the design, we incorporate those skylights into the pattern…



(Claire Mawisa) For years Braam has donated his time, energy and professional talents to the Trust’s projects.



(Braam van der Hoven) The most dramatic patients I've seen is the burns patients in Ngwelezana. The dire need in burns patients is indescribable. It's really, it’s major.



(Claire Mawisa) Ngwelezana Hospital in KwaZulu Natal serves a population of around two and a half million people.



(Karolina Andropoulos) We went to visit Ngwelezana and found the most abject conditions.



(Claire Mawisa) Many of those people live in informal settlements, so burns are common.

(Unnamed mother Subtitles) We were sitting in the dining room and there was boiling water in the bedroom. Then I heard her crying… When I saw her she was burnt.



(Claire Mawisa) Until 2019, children were treated alongside adults in a crowded and dilapidated burns ward.



(Calvin Mkhabela) It’s about restoring dignity and restoring hope to the children and the families that need it the most.



(Claire Mawisa) Calvin Mkhabela is Vice President of Operations at South32’s Hillside Aluminium. Thanks to the company’s R10.3 million capital donation, the Trust built a pediatric inpatient burns unit at Ngwelezana.



(Claire Mawisa) Have you been to a handover?



(Calvin Mkhabela) Yes, I have.



(Claire Mawisa) And how has that been? Maybe you can share that experience.



(Calvin Mkhabela) It's actually very emotional. You walk into a space that is filled with light, that’s filled with colour. And you see the smiles in the children that are being treated in that hospital. You see the relief from the parents knowing that their children are receiving world-class care, the pride from the workers that work in that facility. And that on its own, it's actually moving.



(Benjamin Mokgothu) So it gives them fulfillment that they are able now to save lives instead of saying, “We couldn't make it.



(Claire Mawisa) Benjamin Mokgothu is director of operations at Sakhiwo Health Solutions, which planned health facilities and procured equipment for Ngwelezana - and several other projects.



(Benjamin Mokgothu) It has actually been a very fulfilling partnership. We have more than almost 14 years with the Trust. The one that stands out for me is the burns unit, because a lot of kids were actually dying.



(Claire Mawisa) The inpatient unit was followed by an outpatient unit for children who must return for ongoing care. This year, South32’s generosity also made it possible to donate world class equipment to Ngwelezana.



(Calvin Mkhabela) We believe these facilities is designed to stand the test of time. So, it's a critical part of our legacy that will remain past our lifetime.



(Nomsa Piliso) All the partners that have joined us today, they share the same vision of wanting to do that which is good and better for South Africa.



(Claire Mawisa) On its long journey, the Trust has been humbled by the passion of countless partners.



(Tandy Coleman) Children in hospital is hard. You want a space where they feel happy and then you want a space also where their parents can feel like they are safe and happy as they can be, being in hospital.



(Claire Mawisa) Polysales has provided medical grade vinyl flooring and custom wall art to project after project. Tandy Coleman is the CEO.



(Tandy Coleman) The best part of it is, someone comes up with an idea and then we bring in the floor which is just the sort of palette on which to build. And when I look around here, it’s a beautiful palette on which to build.



(Clinton Soutter) Being a parent myself, I understand what it’s like to have a young child that’s ill.



(Claire Mawisa) Clinton Soutter is national sales manager for Franke, provider of luxury custom stainless-steel ware.



(Clinton Soutter) Our business has got over a hundred years of building products serving this country, and for us to be involved in a project like this is personal.



(Claire Mawisa) And the journey is far from over. George Hospital: a small facility in a picturesque Western Cape town. But the community it serves is vast. Another overstrained government facility. Another opportunity to prove what’s possible - this time, revamping the tiny neonatal ICU and high care unit.



(Rudolf Coetzee) Each project that we take on is quite unique. We see where, where there’s gaps, where there’s need, how they operate. And also, sometimes we question the conventional way of doing stuff.



(Claire Mawisa) Rudolf Coetzee is the architect. He’s a familiar face on the Trust’s projects.



(Claire Mawisa) Do you feel any sense of personal responsibility, understanding that these tiny, fragile little lives will depend on the facility that you have built?



(Rudolf Coetzee) Definitely. But there's also a great relief of the potential that that facility could potentially have on South Africa. You never know where the next big Siya Kolisi will be born, so it might just be in George.



(Tasoulla Hadjigeorgiou) Our ultimate legacy is when someone turns around and said, when I was a child, I received the help I needed from that hospital and someone saved my life. Or someone helped my child.



(Claire Mawisa) LottoStar is the Trust’s biggest single donor: it’s donated R25 million to this project. Tasoulla Hadjigeorgiou is the CEO.



(Tasoulla Hadjigeorgiou) Most people donate and then they go away, right. But to actually be part of something - and it's a three year, it's like watching a child grow.

(Claire Mawisa) It may be the Trust’s newest donor, but already LottoStar has touched lives as principal donor on the Sebokeng Hospital Pediatric Emergency Unit, completed in Gauteng last year.



(Tasoulla Hadjigeorgiou) Actually, we committed to it on the day of the opening of Sebokeng Hospital. We were just taken aback, I think, of everything that we saw. And we shook hands on it, and that was that.



(Claire Mawisa) We're going to get you on the handover from George Hospital. Be ready. There'll be another project, Tas.



(Tasoulla Hajigeorgiou) I'll be there!



(Claire Mawisa) And in the not-too-distant future, a now-familiar sight will unfold.



(Claire Mawisa) The theme of our story is a brick in the wall. What do you understand from that metaphor?



(Nomsa Piliso) I think for me, it really just, the resonance of it is how far you can go together. It's everybody pulling in to say, we want to leave this community better than we found it.



(Calvin Mkhabela) Being part of a foundation that everyone can build on.



(Benjamin Mokgothu) The legacy that we have left behind is something that can be built on by generations to come.



(Braam van der Hoven) That's how you take a R20 million donation and you maximise it to R40 or 45 million.



(Chris Nel) We've tried to ensure that all the bricks were placed in the right position on a proper foundation. Not a foundation with cracks in. And that is what we have achieved.



(Tasoulla Hadjigeorgiou) For us, it's a thank you, but it's a thank you to you for allowing us to be part of a project and acknowledging us that we are part of a project.



(Prof. Kimesh Naidoo) I think this is a prototype, that we can have a sustainable health care system, especially for the public sector and for the most vulnerable, because if we work together, we can actually make a lot of things happen. And I think this is, you know, over these years I've seen that really tangibly happen here.



(Claire Mawisa) The Carte Blanche Making a Difference Trust demonstrates the power of collective public service. It’s a declaration that the care of our children is the most important thing we will ever build together.

Time / Noah Bentfield / Dylan Carter BLINQ 113 ALWAYS MOVING FORWARD PRODUCTION 4 00:01:27 MAMA DANCE Eyal Goldshtein INPIC 062 TX Details Back references from Insert in Show: Title Author Last Updated 21 December 2025 - Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 08 December 2025 TX Date: 0000-00-00 Script: Part 1 (Peter Grealy) These are undeniably world-class facilities. (Benjamin Mokgothu Subtitles) Ours is to create a healing environment and a working space for health professionals to take care of those little ones who need healthcare. (Claire Mawisa) First of its kind facilities, world class care. Would you believe that all of this could be possible behind the unpromising facade of a decades-old government hospital? (Claire Mawisa) But it’s in just such places that a dream has been unfolding for nearly two decades. (Braam van der Hoven) We don't need to fix everything in one go; we can just start. And it will grow. (Claire Mawisa) A dream to provide dedicated, specialist healthcare to children who depend on state hospitals. (Claire Mawisa) Seventeen years on, the Carte Blanche Making a Difference Trust has raised over R200 million, completed 24 projects across 6 provinces, and made a difference to more than 500 000 children. And it all started here, at Charlotte Maxeke Johannesburg Academic Hospital. (Karolina Andropoulos) This is the big deal. For me, this is the big deal. (Dr Tanusha Ramdin) There was nothing here. There was no cubicles. It was completely empty. . (Claire Mawisa) Dr Tanusha Ramdin is head of the neonatal unit. She was a registrar when the Trust built the hospital’s first specialised pediatric unit. (Dr Tanusha Ramdin) I’ve seen the project grow and what a huge impact it’s made on our children. You can see, years later, we’re still working at it. This is our way of preventing the spread of infections. So, it’s made a huge difference. (Claire Mawisa) In 2008, Carte Blanche was celebrating a major milestone. (Derek Watts) Carte Blanche turns 20 this month and there’s a lot to celebrate. But it’s not all about partying. (Claire Mawisa) Then-Executive Producer, George Mazarakis, aimed to mark the anniversary in an unusual way. (George Mazarakis) I think it’s time to press pause on the critical button and to say now’s the time to actually make a difference and say, how can we help? (Claire Mawisa) For Karolina Andropoulos, it was a significant year for a very different reason. (Karolina Andropoulos) I lost a little girl called Georgina. I was terribly moved by, of course, my daughter first, but all the other children I’d seen in state facilities. (Derek Watts) And that’s probably why you identify so strongly with these mothers and their babies, their toddlers. (Karolina Andropoulos) Love them all dearly, they… When you become one of these parents, I think it’s beyond empathy. (Claire Mawisa) Karolina’s daughter Georgina is the muse behind the Trust. She died in April 2008. She was an outpatient at Charlotte Maxeke. (Karolina Andropoulos) I approached George Mazarakis and asked him to join me in this hospital, which he did. And he thereafter, together with a cohort of specialists, founded the Carte Blanche Making a Difference Trust. (George Mazarakis) My dream is to reach R20 million - a million for every year we’ve been on air. I think that would be a meaningful contribution. (Claire Mawisa) And so the first projects took shape. (Narrator) Suspended from the ceiling is the latest in high-definition technology. (Narrator) In Bara’s surgical neonatal unit, the Trust has made a massive impact, revamping the entire area. But it’s not finished yet. (Derek Watts) So Karolina, five ICU beds, what are we looking at? (Karolina Andropoulos) At about R2.5 million please. (Prof. Millind Chitnis) It is really impressive. It is not only of national standard, it is of international standard. (Bongani Bingwa) So this is it? (Gordon Monchu) This is our pediatric ICU for Kimberley Hospital. When I walked in the first time, I couldn’t help myself, I just saw tears rolling down because of the good work and the goodwill that went into this. (Narrator) The Carte Blanche Making a Difference Trust then used half a million rand from viewers to create a comprehensive preschool. (Claire Mawisa) From the very beginning, the Trust has achieved more than anyone could have dreamed. (Claire Mawisa) Did you ever imagine that 200 million would be raised? (Chris Nel) Honestly, nobody expected that to happen. (Claire Mawisa) Chris Nel is the Trust’s financial architect. (Chris Nel) Our expectations were too little. The funds just started rolling in, and we had to ensure that our trust, our methods and our systems, adjusted and was flexible enough to accommodate the growth. (Claire Mawisa) So those were good problems to have. (Chris Nel) Yes, they were good problems to have. (Claire Mawisa) Absolutely. (Claire Mawisa) And what began as a birthday celebration has become nearly eighteen years of touching lives. (Chris Nel) The donors not only gave us money, but they actually gave us trust. (Claire Mawisa) Beyond the balance sheets, what is it like being part of the journey from day one? (Chris Nel) It has been very honoring for me. My whole life I was involved with figures and sums. But this, although it also had to do with the rands and cents, it had a total different meaning. Every decision that we take has a heartbeat behind it. (Peter Grealy) What is unique about the Carte Blanche Making a Difference Trust is that every cent of the capital donations that have been made to us have been applied to our projects. (Claire Mawisa) Peter Grealy has been a Trustee and the Trust’s legal advisor since the very beginning. (Peter Grealy) We've carved out a methodology that ensures that there's no wastage. And that's an important message I think in the South African context, that if you're absolutely focused on the outcome, that it is achievable. (Gladys Bogoshi) Without the partnership of the private sector, the NGOs, we cannot meet our mandate. (Claire Mawisa) Gladys Bogoshi is the CEO of Charlotte Maxeke Academic Hospital. (Gladys Bogoshi) To have this vision in 2011, to build this unit from the shell… (George Mazarakis) This is the very first pediatric specialised ICU in Gauteng, outside of neonatal. (Gladys Bogoshi) …and to come back today. I hope you are proud that it has saved so many lives and it still does. (Dr Tanusha Ramdin) We actually serve, like, half of Gauteng. The patient next door is a trauma patient. The patient next door there is a burns patient. So, we try and accommodate everybody. (Karolina Andropoulos) Fourteen years later, it's still immaculate and in service. And it's enchanting to know that you, as a young baby doctor, a registrar working here 14 years ago, are now the head of neonatology. It's a beautiful thing. (Claire Mawisa) This has always been more than philanthropy. It's the belief that the health of our nation's children is a shared responsibility, and by building these havens of hope, we’re building a healthier future for everyone. Part 2 (Claire Mawisa) In any hospital, there are stories of pain, struggle, and fear. What the Making a Difference Trust sets out to do is to change the endings of those stories. (Nomsa Piliso) So, I mean, stories - the way that we think about storytelling, one is to preserve our history and also to weave ourselves into the national psyche. (Claire Mawisa) MultiChoice’s Nomsa Piliso is a trustee. (Nomsa Piliso) The community in and of itself and corporate should not stand back. If you understand that everybody has a contribution to make, then the model works. (Claire Mawisa) And that’s exactly what unfolded at Victoria Mxenge Hospital in Durban. (Prof. Kimesh Naidoo) Public sector patients are often seen as, oh, they can get something lesser. And this was not done here. We said we’re going to give the kids the best infrastructure there is to offer, and that makes a huge difference. (Dr Kimesh Naidoo) What happened? You woke up now? You woke up? (Claire Mawisa) In 2008, Professor Kimesh Naidoo was simply Doctor Naidoo, a pediatrician at what was then called King Edward VIII. (Dr Kimesh Naidoo) I think looking after sick children in a derelict building which has not been planned appropriately is very dangerous. (Claire Mawisa) It was here, at the hospital where Professor Naidoo still works, that the Trust pulled off one of its most ambitious projects. (George Mazarakis) King Edward stood out head and shoulders above the rest in terms of a place where we needed to intervene to the degree of building a new building, purely because it was so shocking. (Claire Mawisa) The BHP Billiton Pediatric Centre of Excellence was completed in 2012. (Narrator) Gone was the old, cramped outpatients’ area. In its place, a spacious waiting room with a dispensary, clean toilets and consulting rooms attached. (Bongani Bingwa) And that’s the whole point of this hospital, is that these spaces are made to work - not only for the doctors and the nursing staff, but for the patients as well. And these little guys are what it’s all about. Go! (Claire Mawisa) What do you think have been probably the biggest changes that this center has been able to impact on? (Prof. Kimesh Naidoo) The ability to look after children, especially ICU children, children in high care, in a clean, safe environment where they're not packed together, where there's enough equipment. We have treated over 340,000 children who have come in mainly as outpatients and about 10 to 15% of them, just under 35,000, have been admitted. And these are some of the sickest children in the entire province who have had to be admitted here. (Claire Mawisa) Thirteen years later, the centre continues to transform lives - and has provided training to a new generation of pediatric specialists. (Prof. Kimesh Naidoo) There's a pride in the place. It's beautiful. It's a centre of focus in the hospital. We were all sitting in 2012 and you could hear the stories: How long will it last? Will the government manage to keep it going? And I think it's really a team effort that enables something that's donated, something that's given, to be looked after and to fulfill its duty and fulfill its mandate. We’re proud that we've done that. And we will continue to do that. (Claire Mawisa) A child born when these projects began is on the cusp of adulthood. And so is the Trust. But its legacy isn't measured in years - or in money. It’s measured in breaths. In the steady beep of a monitor that’s in a unit that didn’t exist before. (Claire Mawisa) And that legacy is shared by partners both past and present. (Braam van der Hoven) It's wonderful to go back and to see that the upkeep on these facilities is good because there's ownership. (Claire Mawisa) Braam van der Hoven was the lead architect on the Victoria Mxenge project - and many others. (Braam van der Hoven) My function is to balance the requirements of the clinicians with the available budget and space, and then to come up with a design solution that will shorten the length of stay of the patients in these facilities. We sort of do that through natural light and colourful interiors that brings a calming effect to the patients and the caregivers. (Braam van der Hoven) On the design, we incorporate those skylights into the pattern… (Claire Mawisa) For years Braam has donated his time, energy and professional talents to the Trust’s projects. (Braam van der Hoven) The most dramatic patients I've seen is the burns patients in Ngwelezana. The dire need in burns patients is indescribable. It's really, it’s major. (Claire Mawisa) Ngwelezana Hospital in KwaZulu Natal serves a population of around two and a half million people. (Karolina Andropoulos) We went to visit Ngwelezana and found the most abject conditions. (Claire Mawisa) Many of those people live in informal settlements, so burns are common. (Unnamed mother Subtitles) We were sitting in the dining room and there was boiling water in the bedroom. Then I heard her crying… When I saw her she was burnt. (Claire Mawisa) Until 2019, children were treated alongside adults in a crowded and dilapidated burns ward. (Calvin Mkhabela) It’s about restoring dignity and restoring hope to the children and the families that need it the most. (Claire Mawisa) Calvin Mkhabela is Vice President of Operations at South32’s Hillside Aluminium. Thanks to the company’s R10.3 million capital donation, the Trust built a pediatric inpatient burns unit at Ngwelezana. (Claire Mawisa) Have you been to a handover? (Calvin Mkhabela) Yes, I have. (Claire Mawisa) And how has that been? Maybe you can share that experience. (Calvin Mkhabela) It's actually very emotional. You walk into a space that is filled with light, that’s filled with colour. And you see the smiles in the children that are being treated in that hospital. You see the relief from the parents knowing that their children are receiving world-class care, the pride from the workers that work in that facility. And that on its own, it's actually moving. (Benjamin Mokgothu) So it gives them fulfillment that they are able now to save lives instead of saying, “We couldn't make it. (Claire Mawisa) Benjamin Mokgothu is director of operations at Sakhiwo Health Solutions, which planned health facilities and procured equipment for Ngwelezana - and several other projects. (Benjamin Mokgothu) It has actually been a very fulfilling partnership. We have more than almost 14 years with the Trust. The one that stands out for me is the burns unit, because a lot of kids were actually dying. (Claire Mawisa) The inpatient unit was followed by an outpatient unit for children who must return for ongoing care. This year, South32’s generosity also made it possible to donate world class equipment to Ngwelezana. (Calvin Mkhabela) We believe these facilities is designed to stand the test of time. So, it's a critical part of our legacy that will remain past our lifetime. (Nomsa Piliso) All the partners that have joined us today, they share the same vision of wanting to do that which is good and better for South Africa. (Claire Mawisa) On its long journey, the Trust has been humbled by the passion of countless partners. (Tandy Coleman) Children in hospital is hard. You want a space where they feel happy and then you want a space also where their parents can feel like they are safe and happy as they can be, being in hospital. (Claire Mawisa) Polysales has provided medical grade vinyl flooring and custom wall art to project after project. Tandy Coleman is the CEO. (Tandy Coleman) The best part of it is, someone comes up with an idea and then we bring in the floor which is just the sort of palette on which to build. And when I look around here, it’s a beautiful palette on which to build. (Clinton Soutter) Being a parent myself, I understand what it’s like to have a young child that’s ill. (Claire Mawisa) Clinton Soutter is national sales manager for Franke, provider of luxury custom stainless-steel ware. (Clinton Soutter) Our business has got over a hundred years of building products serving this country, and for us to be involved in a project like this is personal. (Claire Mawisa) And the journey is far from over. George Hospital: a small facility in a picturesque Western Cape town. But the community it serves is vast. Another overstrained government facility. Another opportunity to prove what’s possible - this time, revamping the tiny neonatal ICU and high care unit. (Rudolf Coetzee) Each project that we take on is quite unique. We see where, where there’s gaps, where there’s need, how they operate. And also, sometimes we question the conventional way of doing stuff. (Claire Mawisa) Rudolf Coetzee is the architect. He’s a familiar face on the Trust’s projects. (Claire Mawisa) Do you feel any sense of personal responsibility, understanding that these tiny, fragile little lives will depend on the facility that you have built? (Rudolf Coetzee) Definitely. But there's also a great relief of the potential that that facility could potentially have on South Africa. You never know where the next big Siya Kolisi will be born, so it might just be in George. (Tasoulla Hadjigeorgiou) Our ultimate legacy is when someone turns around and said, when I was a child, I received the help I needed from that hospital and someone saved my life. Or someone helped my child. (Claire Mawisa) LottoStar is the Trust’s biggest single donor: it’s donated R25 million to this project. Tasoulla Hadjigeorgiou is the CEO. (Tasoulla Hadjigeorgiou) Most people donate and then they go away, right. But to actually be part of something - and it's a three year, it's like watching a child grow. (Claire Mawisa) It may be the Trust’s newest donor, but already LottoStar has touched lives as principal donor on the Sebokeng Hospital Pediatric Emergency Unit, completed in Gauteng last year. (Tasoulla Hadjigeorgiou) Actually, we committed to it on the day of the opening of Sebokeng Hospital. We were just taken aback, I think, of everything that we saw. And we shook hands on it, and that was that. (Claire Mawisa) We're going to get you on the handover from George Hospital. Be ready. There'll be another project, Tas. (Tasoulla Hajigeorgiou) I'll be there! (Claire Mawisa) And in the not-too-distant future, a now-familiar sight will unfold. (Claire Mawisa) The theme of our story is a brick in the wall. What do you understand from that metaphor? (Nomsa Piliso) I think for me, it really just, the resonance of it is how far you can go together. It's everybody pulling in to say, we want to leave this community better than we found it. (Calvin Mkhabela) Being part of a foundation that everyone can build on. (Benjamin Mokgothu) The legacy that we have left behind is something that can be built on by generations to come. (Braam van der Hoven) That's how you take a R20 million donation and you maximise it to R40 or 45 million. (Chris Nel) We've tried to ensure that all the bricks were placed in the right position on a proper foundation. Not a foundation with cracks in. And that is what we have achieved. (Tasoulla Hadjigeorgiou) For us, it's a thank you, but it's a thank you to you for allowing us to be part of a project and acknowledging us that we are part of a project. (Prof. Kimesh Naidoo) I think this is a prototype, that we can have a sustainable health care system, especially for the public sector and for the most vulnerable, because if we work together, we can actually make a lot of things happen. And I think this is, you know, over these years I've seen that really tangibly happen here. (Claire Mawisa) The Carte Blanche Making a Difference Trust demonstrates the power of collective public service. It’s a declaration that the care of our children is the most important thing we will ever build together.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): As the Trust heads into its 18th year, we celebrate its work and recognise the contributions of donors and partners in its coming of age.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: The Trust turns 18 next year, in 2026. Its latest project (a neonatal unit at George Provincial Hospital) will be completed to coincide with the birthday. We reflect on the lives touched, communities served and stories told. We celebrate the leap of faith that donors and partners make with us, and the idea that all of us are a brick in the wall, contributing towards projects that are always more than the sum of their parts.
metadata.Summary: The Carte Blanche Making a Difference Trust was founded in 2008 for the show’s twentieth birthday. It builds and equips dedicated paediatric facilities in state hospitals, filling gaps in care such as burns treatment, emergency and trauma units, operating theatres, and so on. Behind everything the Trust does is its Patron, Karolina Andropoulos. Her daughter Georgina died aged seven of cancer in 2008, after many years of treatment both in South Africa and in Australia. After her death, Karolina became driven to help create support for South African children in state hospitals similar to what had been available in Australia. Karolina approached George and asked him to tour Charlotte Maxeke’s paediatric unit with her to see what was needed, and so the Trust was born. The initial idea was to raise funds to contribute towards equipment for a local hospital. What it turned into was multiple projects in hospitals all over South Africa - not only equipment donations, but building and equipping operating theatres, centres of excellence and so on. Carte Blanche periodically features the Trust’s work in stories - usually at the handover of a new project - partly because the Trust’s ongoing success and ability to raise funds is dependent on its association with the Carte Blanche brand, and partly to recognise the incredible contributions of donors and partners. Several companies have donated many millions of rands over the past two decades, many of them more than once, and numerous professionals and their companies have donated time, skills and materials.
metadata.Further information: More immediately, the Trust has recently completed three projects at Ngwelezana Hospital in KZN (incidentally, the province is the Trust’s largest beneficiary over time). These are focused on treatment of burns: an inpatient unit, an outpatient unit, and state-of-the-art equipment for testing, cleaning wounds and performing skin grafts. However, there has been increasing difficulty in dealing with the Department of Health in KZN, which has blocked Carte Blanche from hosting a handover of the new facilities to the hospital (and the province). As a result, we have not been able to celebrate our contributors and the finalisation of the project as we usually do. This is primarily why MultiChoice (which is a significant supporter of the Trust’s work, and whose CEO is a Trustee) commissioned a special piece from Carte Blanche to recognise the contribution of the donors and partners in the Ngwelezana projects, to be extended to a celebration of all the people and companies who have contributed over the years. We will interview about 10 “A List” contributors as provided by Karolina. Further details below. In addition we will incorporate “vox pops” from some side characters such as Carte Blanche producers and presenters who have worked on Trust stories, doctors and nurses at the hospitals etc. We will return to two hospitals, hopefully: 1. Charlotte Maxeke, as the site of the genesis of the Trust. The Trust completed a few projects there in its early years (2008-2011): installation of a heart-lung machine, installation of a Lodox digital scanner, and installation of a laparoscopic operating theatre. The operating theatre is still well used and well kept, and we will hopefully return to talk about the impact of this facility on the department. Although staff who were there in 2008-11 have since left, a new generation can use the same facilities to create a better chance for the children in their care. 2. Victoria Mxenge (previously King Edward VIII), Durban, as a representative of KZN and a major focus for the Trust over more than one project. The Trust has contributed equipment to the neonatal nursery, and most importantly, constructed a brand new Paediatric Centre of Excellence (2012). Prof Kimesh Naidoo has worked at the hospital since the Trust’s earliest projects there, and his career has spanned many of the new facilities and capabilities provided by the Trust. He will provide a great legacy interview.
